source: In mice, and to some extent in rats, transgenic tools allow the in vivo detection of particular cell types (Pinto and Dan, 2015; Lui et al., 2021), whereas in vivo studies in primates are largely restricted to using features of the extracellular action potential (EAP) such as trough to peak duration, spike width, and cell firing rate (FR).

source: These experiments introduced the concept of broad- and narrow-spiking neurons.

claim: Later experiments in the guinea pig, cat, and the rat helped establish the idea that broad- and narrow-spiking extracellular waveform shapes mostly corresponded to excitatory and inhibitory cells, respectively.
source: Later experiments in the guinea pig (McCormick et al., 1985), cat (Azouz et al., 1997), and the rat (Simons, 1978; Barthó et al., 2004) then helped establish the idea that these broad- and narrow-spiking extracellular waveform shapes mostly corresponded to excitatory and inhibitory cells, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: These results have been used as the basis for identifying cell types in primate recordings.
source: These results have been used as the basis for identifying cell types in primate recordings (Johnston et al., 2009; Merchant et al., 2008; Merchant et al., 2012).

claim: This method of identifying cell types in mammalian cortex in vivo is widely used in neuroscience but it is insufficient to capture the known structural and transcriptomic diversity of cell types in the monkey and the mouse.
source: This method of identifying cell types in mammalian cortex in vivo is widely used in neuroscience but it is insufficient to capture the known structural and transcriptomic diversity of cell types in the monkey and the mouse (Hodge et al., 2019; Krienen et al., 2020).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent observations in the monkey defy the simple classification of broad- and narrow-spiking cells as corresponding to excitatory and inhibitory cells, respectively.
source: Furthermore, recent observations in the monkey defy this simple classification of broad- and narrow-spiking cells as corresponding to excitatory and inhibitory cells, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a challenge to the traditional classification.

claim: Three examples in the primate that have resisted the principle of broad-spiking as excitatory and narrow-spiking as inhibitory are narrow-spiking pyramidal tract neurons in deep layers of M1 (Betz cells), narrow and broad spike widths among excitatory pyramidal tract neurons of premotor cortex, and narrow-spiking excitatory cells in layer III of V1, V2, and MT.
source: Three such examples in the primate that have resisted this principle are narrow-spiking pyramidal tract neurons in deep layers of M1 (Betz cells, Vigneswaran et al., 2011; Soares et al., 2017), narrow and broad spike widths among excitatory pyramidal tract neurons of premotor cortex (Lemon et al., 2021), and narrow-spiking excitatory cells in layer III of V1, V2, and MT (Constantinople et al., 2009; Amatrudo et al., 2012; Onorato et al., 2020; Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: More recent studies have incorporated additional features of EAPs such as trough to peak duration, repolarization time, and triphasic waveform shape.
source: To capture a more representative diversity of cell types in vivo, more recent studies have incorporated additional features of EAPs (beyond AP width) such as trough to peak duration (Ardid et al., 2015), repolarization time (Trainito et al., 2019; Banaie Boroujeni et al., 2021), and triphasic waveform shape (Barry, 2015; Robbins et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: User-specified methods are insufficient to distinguish between previously identified cell types.
source: Although these user-specified methods are amenable to human intuition, they are insufficient to distinguish between previously identified cell types (Krimer et al., 2005; Vigneswaran et al., 2011; Merchant et al., 2012).

claim: It is unclear how to choose user-specified features in a principled manner as they are often highly correlated with one another.
source: It is also unclear how to choose these user-specified features in a principled manner (i.e. one set that maximizes explanatory power) as they are often highly correlated with one another.

source: This results in different studies choosing between different sets of specified features each yielding different inferred cell classes (Trainito et al., 2019; Viskontas et al., 2007; Katai et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2021).

source: Some studies even conclude that there is no single set of specified features that is a reliable differentiator of type (Weir et al., 2014).

claim: Non-linear dimensionality reduction methods are designed to find patterns in complex datasets.

source: Such methods have seen usage in diverse neuroscientific contexts such as single-cell transcriptomics (Tasic et al., 2018; Becht et al., 2019), in analyzing models of biological neural networks (Maheswaranathan et al., 2019; Kleinman et al., 2019), the identification of behavior (Bala et al., 2020; Hsu and Yttri, 2020; Dolensek et al., 2020), and in electrophysiology (Jia et al., 2019; Gouwens et al., 2020; Klempíř et al., 2020; Markanday et al., 2020; Dimitriadis et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: WaveMAP combines Universal Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) with Louvain community detection.
source: Here, in a novel technique that we term WaveMAP, we combine a non-linear dimensionality reduction method (Universal Manifold Approximation and Projection [UMAP], McInnes et al., 2018) with graph community detection (Louvain community detection, (Blondel et al., 2008); we colloquially call 'clustering') to understand the physiological properties, decision-related dynamics, and laminar distribution of candidate cell types during decision-making.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: WaveMAP significantly outperformed current approaches without need for user-specification of waveform features like trough to peak duration.
source: We found that WaveMAP significantly outperformed current approaches without need for user-specification of waveform features like trough to peak duration.

source: The narrow-spiking set was composed of five clusters with 'narrow-spiking' waveforms (clusters ①, ②, ③, ④, ⑤) and comprised ∼12%, ∼12%, ∼18%, ∼7%, and ∼19% (n = 72, 78, 113, 43, and 116) respectively of the total waveforms, for ∼68% of total waveforms.

source: The broad-spiking set was composed of three 'broad-spiking' waveform clusters (⑥, ⑦, and ⑧) comprising ∼13%, ∼5%, and ∼15% (n = 80, 29, and 94) respectively and collectively ∼32% of total waveforms.

source: The number of clusters identified by WaveMAP is dependent on the resolution parameter for Louvain clustering.

source: A principled way to choose this resolution parameter is to use the modularity score (a measure of how tightly interconnected the members of a cluster are) as the objective function to maximize.

evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the effect of the higher resolution parameter.

evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The features chosen for the GMM were action potential (AP) width of the spike, the peak ratio, and the trough to peak duration.
source: In accordance with previous work, the features we chose (Figure 4A) were action potential (AP) width of the spike (width in milliseconds of the full-width half minimum of the depolarization trough Vigneswaran et al., 2011); the peak ratio the ratio of pre-hyperpolarization peak (A1) to the post-hyperpolarization peak (A2) Barry, 2015; and the trough to peak duration (time in ms from the depolarization trough to post-hyperpolarization peak) which is the most common feature used in analyses of extracellular recordings (Snyder et al., 2016; Kaufman et al., 2013; Merchant et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4A, and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The GMM identified four waveform clusters that roughly separated into broad-spiking (BS, ∼33%, n = 208), narrow-spiking (NS, ∼43%, n = 269), broad-spiking triphasic (BST, ∼9%, n = 55), and narrow-spiking triphasic (NST, ∼15%, n = 93).
source: The result of the GMM applied to these three measures is shown in Figure 4B. This method identified four waveform clusters that roughly separated into broad-spiking (BS, ∼33%, n = 208), narrow-spiking (NS, ∼43%, n = 269), broad-spiking triphasic (BST, ∼9%, n = 55), and narrow-spiking triphasic (NST, ∼15%, n = 93) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Triphasic waveforms are thought to be neurons with myelinated axons or neurites.
source: Triphasic waveforms, thought to be neurons with myelinated axons or neurites (Barry, 2015; Robbins et al., 2013; Deligkaris et al., 2016; Bakkum et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2021), contain an initial positive spike before the trough and can be identified by large peak ratios (Figure 4A).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The GMM clusters are similar to those obtained from other clusterings of EAP's in macaque cortex.
source: These GMM clusters are similar to those obtained from other clusterings of EAP's in macaque cortex (Gur et al., 1999; Trainito et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Four clusters were selected by examining the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) statistic as a function of the number of clusters and identifying the cluster number at the elbow.
source: We selected four clusters by examining the Bayesian information citerion (BIC) statistic as a function of the number of clusters and identified the cluster number at the elbow (green chevron in Figure 4C).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4C.

source: After training, the accuracy across all four classes averaged ∼78% with no classification accuracy over 95% and misclassifications between every class (Figure 4D).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In WaveMAP, the individual classification accuracy of most classes exceeded 95% with few misclassifications between groups even though there were double the number of clusters.
source: In WaveMAP, the individual classification accuracy of most classes exceeded 95% with few misclassifications between groups even though there were double the number of clusters.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section comparing the two classifiers.

source: This result suggests that the clusters based on specified features are less differentiable than WaveMAP clusters even when a much lower cluster number is considered.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section as an interpretation of the classifier performance.

claim: The deficit in GMM performance can be understood as an inability of the GMM to fully capture the latent structure of the data.
source: This deficit can be understood as an inability of the GMM to fully capture the latent structure of the data.

source: Even if the GMM is instantiated with eight clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), a classifier is still unable to generalize this clustering with even modest accuracy (average of 56% across clusters; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) even if the waveforms shapes found by the GMM with eight clusters seem somewhat sensible (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).

source: WaveMAP yielded mappings that were more generalizable than a GMM on features across every number of clusters and both parameters investigated.

source: Thus, it is a deficit of the GMM on constructed feature-based approach to capture the full diversity of waveforms, especially at high cluster number, and not a peculiarity of the model parameters chosen or number of clusters induced.

source: Here, WaveMAP is able to recapitulate the same structure observed by specified features as a gradient from broad- to narrow-spiking along the UMAP-1 direction.

source: If a GMM were used, ② would be split between two classes despite it having a distinct waveform shape characterized by a small pre-hyperpolarization peak, a moderate post-hyperpolarization peak, and relatively constant repolarization slope.

source: Second, we leverage the gradient boosted decision tree classifier in Figure 3C and used a decision tree implementation (path-dependent TreeSHAP Lundberg et al., 2018) of SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP values Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020) to reveal what waveform features are implicitly used to differentiate clusters.

evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: As UMAP-1 increases, there is a smooth transition in the sign of the inflection of the repolarization slope (the second derivative) from negative to positive (slow to fast repolarization rate).
source: As UMAP-1 increases, there is a smooth transition in the sign of the inflection of the repolarization slope (the second derivative) from negative to positive (slow to fast repolarization rate).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the inverse UMAP transform.

claim: The post-hyperpolarization peak becomes more sharp as we increase in the UMAP-1 direction.
source: That is, the post-hyperpolarization peak becomes more sharp as we increase in the UMAP-1 direction.

source: As UMAP-2 increases, we see a widening of the post-hyperpolarization slope distinct from the change in its inflection (UMAP-1).

source: These two UMAP dimensions recapitulate the known importance of hyperpolarization properties in clustering waveforms.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section as an interpretation of the inverse UMAP transform.

claim: Both hyperpolarization rate (proportional to trough to peak width) and hyperpolarization slope inflection (proportional to repolarization time) are separate but highly informative properties.
source: Both hyperpolarization rate (proportional to trough to peak width) and hyperpolarization slope inflection (proportional to repolarization time) are separate but highly informative properties (Trainito et al., 2019; Ardid et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Since repolarization rate and post-hyperpolarization width associate with different UMAP dimensions, this implies that these two processes are somewhat independent factors shaping the waveform.
source: Furthermore, since repolarization rate and post-hyperpolarization width associate with different UMAP dimensions, this implies that these two processes are somewhat independent factors shaping the waveform.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section as an interpretation of the inverse UMAP transform.

claim: Repolarization rates are governed by potassium channel dynamics and may play an important role in waveform shape.
source: Repolarization rates are goverened by potassium channel dynamics and may play an important in waveform shape (Soares et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section and supported by a citation to prior literature.

evidence: Directly stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5B, and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SHAP values build off of the game theoretic quantity of Shapley values, which poses that each feature (point in time along the waveform) is of variable importance in influencing the classifier to decide whether the data point belongs to a specific class or not.
source: SHAP values build off of the game theoretic quantity of Shapley values (Shapley, 1988; Štrumbelj and Kononenko, 2014), which poses that each feature (point in time along the waveform) is of variable importance in influencing the classifier to decide whether the data point belongs to a specific class or not.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SHAP values are calculated by examining the change in classifier performance as each feature is obscured (the waveform's amplitude at each time point in this case), one-by-one.
source: Operationally, SHAP values are calculated by examining the change in classifier performance as each feature is obscured (the waveform's amplitude at each time point in this case), one-by-one (Lundberg and Lee, 2017).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Not every time point is equally informative for distinguishing every cluster individually.
source: It is important to note that not every time point is equally informative for distinguishing every cluster individually and thus each bar is subdivided into the mean absolute SHAP value contribution of the eight constituent waveform classes.
evidence: Directly stated in the results section describing the SHAP values.

claim: The 0.7 ms location is highly informative for cluster ⑤ and the 0.3 ms point is highly informative for cluster ⑦.
source: For instance, the 0.7 ms location is highly informative for cluster ⑤ and the 0.3 ms point is highly informative for cluster ⑦ (Figure 5C).

source: Similarly, SHAP values implicate the region around 0.3 ms to 0.4 ms as time points that are also of importance and these correspond to the pre-hyperpolarization peak which is notably able to partition out triphasic waveforms (Barry, 2015).

source: This result suggests that using only up to 1.0 ms or less of the waveform may obscure diversity.

source: These individually informative features often do align with those identified as globally-informative but do so with cluster-specific weights. Put another way, not every time point is equally informative for identifying waveforms individually and these 'most informative' parts of each waveform do not always perfectly align with globally informative features.

source: The broad-spiking clusters ⑥ and ⑦ were not significantly different but both differed significantly from ⑧ in that their baseline FR was much higher (10.3 ± 0.7 and 13.2 ± 1.9 spikes/s vs. 7.6 ± 0.75 spikes/s [median ± bootstrap S.E.]; p = 0.0052, p = 0.0029 respectively, Mann-Whitney U test, FDR adjusted).

source: The narrow-spiking clusters (Figure 6B, right) ②, ③, and ④ had relatively low median baseline FRs (7.5 ± 1.1, 7.4 ± 0.4, 6.5 ± 0.7 spikes/s, median ± bootstrap S.E.) and were not significantly different from one another but all were significantly different from ① and ⑤ (p = 0.04, p = 2.8e-4, p = 2.8e-7, p = 4.9e-5, respectively, Mann-Whitney U test, FDR adjusted; see Figure 6C).
